newsitem.title: USA: Clinton campaigns in key state of Florida.
newsitem.headline: Clinton campaigns in key state of Florida.

text.p: President Bill Clinton, hoping to end a two-decades-old Republican stranglehold over Florida's presidential voting, has been stressing his stands on education, the environment and health care to woo voters.

With a new nationwide poll taken for Reuters showing that most voters trust Clinton over Republican rival Bob Dole on a broad range of issues, the Democratic president on Friday was wrapping up two days of campaigning in the voter-rich state -- convinced he may win its votes in the Nov. 5 election.

The poll, conducted for Reuters by John Zogby International, found Clinton leading Dole by 48.2 percent to 33.3 percent, with 5.9 percent selecting Reform candidate Ross Perot. It also found Clinton has amassed a wide lead over Dole when it comes to handling issues most voters say are important to them.
On education issues, 55.4 percent of voters favoured Clinton, compared to 25.4 percent who backed Dole and 6.2 percent who trusted Texas billionaire Perot.

On health care, Clinton was favoured 48.7 percent to 27.7 percent for Dole, while Perot trailed with 5.2 percent. Clinton held a similar wide lead on dealing with environmental issues, with 51.1 percent of voters comfortable with him while 19.2 percent chose Dole. Perot was backed by 3.2 percent.
Clinton campaign officials said it was no coincidence the president was stressing those themes in his appearances. "We feel that our message is doing very well," said campaign spokesman Joe Lockhart.
Internal campaign polling shows Clinton slightly ahead in Florida, whetting the president's appetite to try and become the first Democratic candidate to win the state since Jimmy Carter in 1976.

In Orlando, Clinton was to address the 116th annual National Baptist Convention, one of the world's largest black religious organisations, and address students and faculty at Valencia Community College. He also was to attend a Democratic National Committee luncheon expected to raise $200,000.
He also planned to visit Panama City to speak at Gulf Coast Community College and attend a political reception before returning to Washington late Friday night.

On Thursday, in Sunshine, Fla., Clinton announced the creation of a new commission that will study the financing and quality of American health care in a rapidly changing system and report to the president next year.

In Washington, House Republican leader Dick Armey and others were quick to criticise the new commission -- calling it a warmed over version of the group headed by Clinton's wife, Hillary, that produced the failed 1993 plan to provide health insurance for all Americans.
Armey warned of a government controlled health care system -- an argument Republicans used to turn public opinion against Clinton's health reform plan.
Representative Dan Miller, a Florida Republican, said "Bill Clinton is so far ahead in the polls he thinks the real Bill Clinton can start coming out. He's going back to the liberal base he had."

Dole needs to hang on to Florida if he is to have any chance of upsetting the Democratic president on Nov. 5. Two of his top strategists, Don Sipple and Mike Murphy, quit his faltering campaign on Thursday in what the Dole camp called a friendly departure.
